title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
This page ends E719 (Nova Acta XIV, 1805), Euler's paper on 'idoneal numbers' (numeri idonei). A number N is idoneal if every number that is represented in exactly one way as N x^2 + y^2 (with gcd(Nx, y) = 1) is prime, or the double of a prime, or a prime power. Euler uses these numbers to certify large primes.

(i) End of the 'alia demonstratio' (§§79-80). Let 2i be idoneal with i odd. Suppose a composite C = 8i f^2 + b^2. Because 2i is idoneal, C has a second representation 2i c^2 + d^2. Then 2i(4f^2 - c^2) = d^2 - b^2. Since b and d are odd, the right side is divisible by 8. Since i is odd, this forces 4 | 4f^2 - c^2, so c is even, c = 2g. Hence C = 8i g^2 + d^2 is a second representation in the 8i form. So a number represented only once by 8i x^2 + y^2 is prime, and 8i is idoneal. In other words, N ≡ 2 (mod 4) idoneal implies 4N idoneal.

(ii) §81, observations on the table of the 65 idoneal numbers (1 ... 1848):
1°. The only primes in the table are 2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 37. Euler conjectures that 37 is the last, because larger idoneal numbers involve ever more factors.
2°. Doubles of primes in the table are 4(?), 6, 10, 22, 58; 58 is the last.
3°. Prime squares (and 16) in the table are 4, 9, 16, 25.
4°. Euler lists the idoneal numbers with exactly two 'simple' factors, where powers of 2, prime squares and doubles of primes count as simple: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 28, 30, 40, 42, 48, 57, 70, 45, 78, 85, 93, 102, 112, 130, 133, 177, 190, 232, 253. All others have three or more factors. This supports the conjecture that idoneal numbers acquire more and more factors.
5°. 1 through 10 are all idoneal, then the numbers thin out. There are gaps 520-760, 840-1320 and 1365-1848.
6°. Euler found no idoneal number between 1848 and 4000.
7°. Euler argues there is no even-even (≡ 0 mod 4) idoneal number up to 16000, because its quarter would be idoneal and below 4000. He finds odd and ≡ 2 (mod 4) idoneal numbers in (4000, 16000) 'most improbable', concludes 1848 is truly the last, and calls this an 'insigne paradoxon', since the numbers are generated by a law that seems to go on forever.

Modern reading: N is idoneal iff the form class group of discriminant -4N has exponent ≤ 2 (one class per genus, Gauss). Then h(-4N) = 2^(t-1) for t = number of genera. Since h grows like sqrt(N) (Siegel), N must have ever more prime factors. This is exactly the explanation of Euler's empirical 'more factors' observation.
errors: §81.7 relies on the converse of the proven theorem: that an idoneal number ≡ 0 (mod 4) has an idoneal quarter. Only 'N ≡ 2 mod 4 idoneal ⇒ 4N idoneal' (and 2i ⇒ 8i) was proved. The converse is true (genus theory / class group of discriminant -16m versus -4m), and it holds for every multiple of 4 in his table, but Euler does not prove it here.
The list in 4° is incomplete under Euler's own conventions. 33 = 3·11, 72 = 8·9 (power of 2 times prime square) and 88 = 8·11 are idoneal two-factor numbers and are omitted.

The conventions in 4° are inconsistent. Doubles of primes (6, 10) are treated as single factors in 3.6, 4.6, 7.10 etc., while '2 itself is rejected'. The '2.2' in 2° is presumably 4, which is also counted among the squares.
The finiteness conclusion (1848 is last) is heuristic. It remains unproved: Weinberger (1973) showed at most one further idoneal number exists, and none under GRH.
Minor gap in §79: b and d are claimed odd because they must be coprime to 2i. For composite C this needs the primitive-representation convention, which is implicit.

ideas.what: If 2i (i odd) is idoneal then 8i is idoneal (second proof via a parity/mod 8 argument)
ideas.modern_name: Idoneal N ≡ 2 mod 4 implies 4N idoneal; relation between class groups of discriminants -4N and -16N
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E719, E708 circle); later treated by Grube (1874) and in Kani's survey
ideas.where_published: E719 §§77-80; related idoneal papers E708, E725

ideas.what: Empirical observation that idoneal numbers must have more and more prime factors; only primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 37
ideas.modern_name: Exponent-≤2 class groups: h(-4N) = 2^(t-1) together with Siegel's lower bound for h
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss (genus theory, one class per genus); Chowla (1934) for finiteness; Weinberger (1973)
ideas.where_published: E719 §81; discussed in Kani, 'Idoneal numbers and some generalizations' (2011)

ideas.what: Using the 4N-theorem to push the search bound from 4000 to 16000 for multiples of 4
ideas.modern_name: Reduction of idoneal multiples of 4 to N/4

ideas.what: Conjecture that 1848 is the last idoneal number; the 'paradox' of a lawlike sequence being finite
ideas.modern_name: Completeness of Euler's list of 65 idoneal numbers (open; at most one more; none under GRH)
ideas.where_published: E719, E725 and Euler's correspondence with Fuss/Beguelin

missed.claim: Euler's tabulation of two-factor idoneal numbers omits 33, 72 and 88, which qualify under his stated conventions. This is a minor slip, probably unnoted, but of no mathematical consequence.
missed.quote: Tales numeros tabula nostra offert sequentes: 4.3, 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, ...
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only for accurate historical commentary on Euler's statistics of idoneal factors.

deep.surprise_reason: The content (8i theorem, the prime and factor observations, 1848 as last, finiteness paradox) is well known and discussed in the histories of idoneal numbers (Dickson, Kani). Euler's 'more factors' heuristic anticipates the genus-theory explanation, but this is already recognized. Only minor unnoted slips.
transcription_corrections: Header on p.51 reads 'Tom. XIIII' (roman numeral form for XIV), as printed.
'10.13' at the top of p.51 repeats the catchword at the foot of p.50; it is not a duplicate entry.
In 2° the first item, transcribed '2.2[?]', is unclear in the scan. Context suggests 2·2 = 4, but this is uncertain.
Footer 'Nova Acta Acad. Imp. Scient. Tom. XIV. G' belongs to the previous page; this page ends with signature 'G 2' and catchword 'OB-'.
